newsitem.title: SPAIN: FEATURE - Spaniards gamble up to a month's wage annually.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Spaniards gamble up to a month's wage annually.

text.p: Every day millions of Spaniards cross their fingers that today will be the perfect day -- the day they become a millionaire.
Every year the average Spaniard spends more than 80,000 pesetas ($548), more than the minimum monthly wage, buying lottery tickets and playing bingo or slot machines.
They shell out more money on games of chance than any other country in Europe, followed by France whose gross domestic product per capita is at least 50 percent higher.
"Spain is certainly at the top of the list of European countries in terms of expenditure on the lottery," said Bernard Podlers, director of the European Gaming Institute in The Hague.
Gambling causes no controversy in Spain as it has in other countries because it is a very traditional habit.

What makes Spain Europe's kingdom of gambling addiction is the huge, tax-free prizes on offer and a spectacular range of games which allow everyone from teenagers to pensioners to bet almost every day of the year.
Money prizes range from the recovery of your bet to record highs of more than two billion pesetas ($13.7 million).
SPAIN OFFERS CORNUCOPIA FOR DISCRIMINATING GAMBLERS
Gamblers can play a variety of lotteries -- from ONCE to the Primitiva, to the Bonoloto, or the quiniela which is tied to Spain's beloved soccer results.
The Primitiva, or primitive, was the first introduced in Spain in around 1760. It was suspended when the National Lottery, launched in 1812, proved more successful.

In 1985, the Primitiva was reintroduced with a draw each Thursday and Saturday. The state also introduced Bonoloto, which works on a similar system of betting on six numbers out of 50 (from numbers one to 49) but at a lower cost.
Bonoloto has draws on Monday, Wednesday and Friday.
While other games show a more dynamic sales trend, the National Lottery, based on a simple ticket system, is still the most popular with 1996 sales of 563 billion pesetas.

In the week before Christmas alone, the National Lottery's Gordo, "The Fat One", sold 200 billion pesetas in tickets. In this draw, gamblers vie for a special prize of 300 million pesetas that can be won by more than one person.
"The maximum is a series of 117 tickets with the same number which mean a total prize of 37 billion pesetas," a spokesman for the National Lottery said.
But lotteries are just one option. Spaniards can find slot machines almost anywhere, from bars to shops to railway or bus stations.
SPECIAL LOTTERY FOR THE BLIND ORIGINATED BY FRANCO

Out of total expenditure on gambling, 49 percent goes to private games, around 32 percent to state lotteries and the remaining 19 percent is spent on the private group National Organisation for Spanish Blind People (ONCE).
In 1938, during the Civil War, Spanish dictator Francisco Franco allowed a group of blind former soldiers to sell lottery tickets in order to support themselves.
ONCE is now one of the biggest non-profit organisations in the country, with 1997 turnover of 386 billion pesetas based on the sale of lottery tickets.
As democracy took root after Franco's 1975 death, "Spain opened up to games, with bingo, casino and slot machines," said Jose Antonio Montero, director of ONCE, himself blind.
"Our clients spend money on the lottery mainly because they hope to win, but also as a kind of vice and because they know what our association is doing," Montero added.
Despite Spain's love for soccer, the Quiniela, which is tied to soccer results, receives only seven percent of the total money spent on gambling.
"With the Quiniela...you have a big amount of small-time gamblers, playing in the hope of winning but also because they like soccer," Montero said.

But the Quinela is also proving increasingly dynamic in terms of sales, said the spokesman of the state department which manages the National Lotteries. Sales rose to 70 billion pesetas in 1997 from 62 billion in 1996.
"In the last three to four years the Quinela has been the one which increased sales the most," the National Lottery spokesman said. In 1996, the Quinela had record prize money of 1.4 billion pesetas.
ASTRONOMICAL LOTTERY PRIZES A BIG INCENTIVE
Astonishingly high prizes are naturally the biggest incentive behind the Spaniards' affection for the lotteries.
Prizes not won are accumulated in a jackpot, known as the BOTE, which mushrooms into huge sums of money.

Only this month, a lucky winner in the northwestern city of Salamanca won a 968 million peseta jackpot for his 2,800-peseta ticket. A record high of 2.2 billion pesetas was won in 1994 on the Primitiva.
"By spending around 1,000 pesetas you can win up to 500 million pesetas each Saturday," the lottery spokesman said. ($ = 145.9 Spanish Pesetas)
